1:1.t: According to the Seventy translators, in the order of the twelve prophets Nahum is placed after Jonah, because they seem to prophesy about the same city. For it is written in Jonah: The word of the Lord came to Jonah, son of Amittai, saying: Arise and go to Nineveh, the great city, and preach in it. But in Nahum this is the opening: The taking up of Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite. Therefore both weave their prophecy about Nineveh, the metropolis of the Assyrians, which is now called Ninus. Moreover, in the Hebrew, Micah is placed after Jonah, and Micah is followed by Nahum, which means consoler. […]

The burden of Nineveh, the book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite. First, he defines the purpose of the prophecy, and usefully clarifies what and where it looks to; then he makes clear who is speaking and from where. For he says "burden," that is, the prophecy that has been received and set forth and is at hand would be understood not about any others, but against Nineveh, or in other words, let the burden of the prophecy be understood as Nineveh. And the book is inscribed "The Vision of Nahum of Elkosh." This is doubtless a village somewhere in the land of the Jews. For we shall take 'of Elkosh' not as from a father, but rather as from a place. And we say this, having the tradition from the readings.

1:2.t: A jealous God, and an avenging Lord. The voice of the prophet praising God because he has avenged on the Assyrians the wrong done to his people. Or, according to a higher understanding, because he hears the groaning of his saints, and at the consummation of the world makes the adversaries feel punishments. That zeal is taken in a good sense, the apostle Paul too shows, saying: Be zealous for the greater gifts, and in another place: For I am zealous for you with the zeal of God, and the Lord himself in the psalm: The zeal of your house has consumed me, and Elijah: Zealous, he says, I have been zealous for the Lord Almighty, the God of Israel. We read also of the zeal of Phinehas, and of Mattathias. […]

God is jealous and the Lord avenges; the Lord avenges with wrath; the Lord avenges his adversaries, and he cuts off his enemies. The Lord is long-suffering and his strength is great, and he will by no means clear the guilty. The saying is profound, and not easy to grasp, except only for those who are willing to examine closely the things in it. And if it should be understood as having been directed to the Jews, we will find the exhortation suitably mixed with moderate rebuke. But if someone should think it was made and spoken against Nineveh, the mind will be turned to another of the interpretations, and to those who have suffered the devastation it gives and confirms the hopes of recovering again. We shall therefore make the purpose of the meaning for both as clear as possible. […]

1:3.t: And again: "I will reestablish my covenant with you, and you shall know that I am Lord, that you may remember and be confounded and may no more open your mouth because of your confusion, when I shall be pacified toward you for all that you have done, says the Lord God." Thus it is clearly indicated by these divine words what was meant in another place by the statement "And though cleansing you he shall not make you innocent." Even the just, being restored to their former state after committing sin, do not dare open their mouth but say with the apostle, "I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God."

The Lord is patient and great in strength, and, cleansing, he will not make innocent. This is said more expressively in the Greek: καὶ ἀθῳῶν οὐκ ἀθῳώσει (and clearing he will not clear). And the sense is: he was indeed long patient with the crime of the Assyrians, and by the strength of his magnanimity bore their iniquities, calling them to repentance; but since, having despised the goodness of God, according to their impenitent heart they stored up for themselves wrath on the day of wrath, he who before was patient will by no means allow them to go away unpunished as though clean and innocent. […]

The Lord's way is in destruction and in shaking, and clouds are the dust of his feet. As the Prophet is about to proclaim beforehand the capture of Nineveh for the comfort of those who have suffered, and to make clear to the wronged that it will be shaken down by God, he usefully recounts first the all-powerful nature of the divine, and that for it, when it chooses to accomplish anything whatsoever, there is nothing that resists, but rather everything follows easily, and what seems good to it will prevail, even if some earthly matter seems difficult for us and for those like us to accomplish. For the Jews thought that the Babylonians would be most difficult to capture, and possessed a hand so invincible, that not even if God wished it, could they be weak against their enemies. […]

1:4.t: If it is [Marcion's] Christ that is meant, he will not be stronger than the servants of the Creator. I would have been content with the examples I have shown you without adding anything further. But here a prediction of [Christ] walking on the water precedes his advent as well. The words of the psalm are, in fact, accomplished by Christ's crossing over the lake. "The Lord," says the psalmist, "is upon many waters." When he scatters its waves, Habakkuk's words are fulfilled where he says, "scattering the waters as he walks." When at his rebuke the sea is calmed, Nahum is also verified: "He rebukes the sea and makes it dry," referring to the winds that had disturbed the sea.

Rebuking the sea, and drying it up, and leading all the rivers to the desert. According to the letter, the power of God is described: since he is about to vindicate Israel against its adversaries, it is no great thing for him to destroy the Assyrians, whose majesty is such that he can even change the elements. Or certainly, since we have said once for all that the prophecy concerns the consummation of the world, take this too in the simple sense. When the consummation of the world comes, and heaven and earth pass away, the sea too and the rivers are dried up. But to me, as I read that passage in the psalms: This great and wide sea, there are creeping things without number, small animals with great. […]

And the Prophet said, "He rebuketh the sea, and maketh it dry, and drieth up all the rivers;" and again, "He looketh on the earth and it trembleth; He rebuketh the mountains, and they smoke." And again the prophet Isaiah saith, "All the nations are accounted as nothing by Him." Now these things the Spirit of God spake concerning the power of God, that those things which were not He called to come into existence, and that what did exist He called and changed into nothing. To this power also He compareth faith.

1:5.t: The mountains were moved by him, and the hills were made desolate, and the earth trembled before his face, and the world, and all who dwell in it. LXX: The mountains were moved by him, and the hills were shaken, and the earth shrank back before his face, the universe and all who dwell in it. It can also be taken simply: that at the consummation of the world, when the Savior comes in his majesty, the mountains and hills, the world and the earth, and all things are moved. For if at his passion the sun fled, the rocks were split, the earth trembled, much more will all things be thrown into turmoil at his glory. […]

1:6.t: Before the face of his indignation who will stand, and who will resist in the wrath of his fury? LXX: From the face of his wrath who will endure, and who will resist in the wrath of his fury? In place of what we have put: And who will resist in the wrath of his fury? Symmachus translated more plainly: And who will endure the wrath of his fury? Therefore one will be found rarely, or not at all, who is not deserving of the wrath that rebukes. Nor will there be any soul that does not tremble at the judgment of God, since even the stars are not clean in his sight. […]

1:7.t: Good is the Lord, and strengthening in the day of tribulation, and knowing those who hope in him. LXX: Sweet is the Lord to those who wait for him in the day of tribulation, and recognizing those who fear him. When he has begun to be angry with the nations and to lay waste kingdoms once most powerful, he will know those who are his, and will not overwhelm those at sea in one and the same storm. But let us understand the day of tribulation, according to ἀναγωγὴν (anagogy), as the day of judgment, of which Isaiah wrote: Behold, the day of the Lord comes, incurable, of fury and of wrath, to make the world a desert and to destroy sinners out of it. […]

1:8.t: And in a flood passing by he will make a consummation of its place, and darkness will pursue his enemies. LXX: And in a flood passing over he will make a consummation; darkness will pursue those rising up and his enemies. The Lord is patient and of great mercy, and he will not be angry to the end, nor will he be indignant forever; but when wickedness has grown upon the earth, and all flesh has corrupted its way, he will bring on a flood that is to pass through, not to remain forever. […]

1:9.t: This, that according to the law, for example, the "adulterer or adulteress" was punished with present death: on account of this very thing, that he bore the penalty of his sin and paid the worthy punishments of the crime committed, what will there be after this that threatens vengeance to their souls, if they have transgressed in nothing else, if there is no other sin which condemns them, but they committed this alone and only then, when they were punished and bore the punishment of the law for this? "The Lord will not take vengeance twice for the same thing"; for they received back their sin and the penalty of the crime is consumed. […]

A deacon who commits fornication after his appointment to the diaconate is to be deposed. But, after he has been rejected and ranked among the laity, he is not to be excluded from communion. For there is an ancient canon that those who have fallen from their degree are to be subjected to this kind of punishment alone.

Herein, as I suppose, the ancient authorities followed the old rule “Thou shalt not avenge twice for the same thing.” There is this further reason too, that laymen, when expelled from the place of the faithful, are from time to time restored to the rank whence they have fallen; but the deacon undergoes once for all the lasting penalty of deposition. His deacon’s orders not being restored to him, they rested at this one punishment.
Clerics who are guilty of the sin unto death are degraded from their order, but not excluded from the communion of the laity. Thou shalt not punish twice for the same fault.

What are you plotting against the Lord? He himself will make a consummation; a twofold tribulation will not rise up. LXX: What are you plotting against the Lord? He himself will make a consummation, he will not avenge twice on the same thing in tribulation. Symmachus more plainly: They will not withstand the onset of a second distress; Theodotion: A second tribulation will not rise up. But according to tropology he is speaking against Marcion, of whom we spoke above, and against all the old heretics, who, inventing some good God or other, say that he is the one who will make the consummation of the world, and accuse the God of the law as if of cruelty, because he punishes many and inflicts torments for sins. What then, he says, are you plotting against the Lord? […]

Moreover, since, having been taught by the Hebrews, we wish to follow their tradition too, and to set out for our own, that is, for Christians, an explanation of the history, it must be said: A twofold tribulation will not rise up, that is, the two tribes will not be captured by the Assyrians as the ten were captured. For while the Assyrians are still in the land of Judah, and like thorns embrace one another, glad and rejoicing, they will be consumed by the angel, when in one night one hundred and eighty-five thousand of the enemy were slain. […]

1:10.t: For as thorns embrace one another, so is their banquet of men drinking together; it will be consumed like stubble full of dryness. LXX: For even to their foundations they will be reduced into brambles, and like bindweed wound about it will be devoured, and like stubble full of dryness. The three distinctions which the Lord set down in the parable of the sowing, apart from the good soil, which bears fruit thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold, the prophet seems to me to unfold again: one, the seed that fell beside the way, another that fell among stones, and a third that fell among thorns; and the Apostle too, speaking of those who do not build well upon the foundation of Christ, indeed intimates this, that there are some who build wood, hay, stubble. […]

1:11.t: For out of you will go forth one plotting wickedness against the Lord, turning over transgression in his mind. LXX: Out of you will go forth a thought against the Lord, most evil, thinking contrary things. Truly from the heretics will go forth a thought hostile to the Lord. Does it not seem to be wickedness and transgression against God to say, as Valentinus does, that the Creator was brought forth last, as if the abortion of an erring Wisdom? Is not the shamelessness of Basilides a thought against God, and the monstrous name ἄβραξας (Abraxas), which is set above the Lord the Maker?

1:12.t: Thus says the Lord: If they are complete, and so more numerous, even so they will be shorn, and he will pass through; I have afflicted you, and I will not afflict you any more; and now I will break his rod from your back, and I will burst your bonds. LXX: Thus says the Lord, reigning over many waters: and so they will be divided, and your report will not be heard any more; and now I will break his rod from you, and I will burst his bonds. According to the letter the sense is plain: Although, he says, the Assyrians are strong, and their might is increased by the number of all the nations, even so, as the angel lays waste, they are shorn. […]

But according to the LXX the sense is far different. For he still seems to be speaking against those to whom he had said above: What are you plotting against the Lord? and: Out of you will go forth a thought against the Lord, most evil, thinking contrary things. Thus, then, says the Lord, reigning over many waters, that is, over the powers, which are called the waters above the heavens, and which are commanded to praise the Lord, or else over the understandings and the wisdom and the teachings of God. […]

1:13.t: Finally he adds: And now I will break his rod, that is, the Assyrian's, from your back, and I will burst your bonds; either signifying his power by a metaphor, or else the rod with which he was trying to strike, and the bonds which he was preparing for the captives; although the siege of the shut-in multitude can also be taken for the bonds.

But this too, which he adds: And now I will break his rod from you, and I will burst your bonds, is said on behalf of the very ones against whom the threat is made, that they may by no means be beaten by the devil, nor be subject to him at whose instigation they had devised and fabricated such great things. Therefore his dominion over them will be broken, and the bonds by which the souls of sinners were bound will be burst by the word of God, saying to those who are in bonds: Go out.

1:14.t: And the Lord will command against you: It shall not be sown from your name any more. From the house of your god I will slay the graven and the molten image; I will make your grave, for you are without honor. LXX: And the Lord will command concerning you: It shall not be sown from your name any more. From the house of your god I will destroy the graven images and the molten images, I will make your grave, for they are swift; behold upon the mountains the feet of one who brings good news and announces peace. I have set down more from the Seventy translators for this reason, that the second περικοπὴ (pericope) could not be separated from the first. […]

But according to the Seventy translators, join what follows to what precedes: It shall not be sown, he says, from your name any more. By no means, O heretics, will the souls of the deceived take from your dogmas the names which they had previously invoked upon their lands, as is sung figuratively in the forty-eighth (49th) psalm. And this very cessation of sowing will profit you, a sowing which used to kill first the soul of the sower, then that of him in whom he sowed. The dogmas of errors, therefore, will die for you; and you too, who before seemed to yourself to be alive, will die to error, and, dead for your own good, you will have as your grave the idols which you used to worship. […]

The prophet Nahum (or, better, God speaking through him) says, "I will destroy the graven and molten thing; I will make it your grave. Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that brings peace. O Judah, keep your festivals and pay your vows, for it shall no longer be that they may pass into disuse. It is completed, it is consumed, it is taken away. He is come up that breathes into your face and rescues you from tribulation." Anyone who knows the Gospels will recognize who it was that came up from hell and breathed the Holy Spirit into the face of Judah, that is, into the face of his Jewish disciples. The words about the festivals are, of course, a reference to the New Testament, in which festivals are so spiritually renewed that they can never "pass into disuse." […]

1:15.t: Now again, my beloved, has God brought us to the season of the feast, and through His loving-kindness we have reached the period of assembly for it. For that God who brought Israel out of Egypt, even He at this time calls us to the feast, saying by Moses, ‘Observe the month of new fruits, and keep the Passover to the Lord thy God:’ and by the prophet, ‘Keep thy feasts, O Judah; pay to the Lord thy vows.’ If then God Himself loves the feast, and calls us to it, it is not right, my brethren, that it should be delayed, or observed carelessly; but with alacrity and zeal we should come to it, so that having begun joyfully here, we may also receive an earnest of that heavenly feast.

Now observe; that city, since the coming of our Saviour, has had an end, and all the land of the Jews has been laid waste; so that from the testimony of these things (and we need no further proof, being assured by our own eyes of the fact) there must, of necessity, be an end of the shadow. And not from me should these things be learned, but the sacred voice of the prophet foretold, crying; ‘Behold upon the mountains the feet of Him that bringeth good tidings, and publisheth peace;’ and what is the message he published, but that which he goes on to say to them, ‘Keep thy feasts, O Judah; pay to the Lord thy vows. For they shall no more go to that which is old; it is finished; it is taken away: He is gone up who breathed upon the face, and delivered thee from affliction.’ […]

Behold upon the mountains the feet of him who brings good tidings and announces peace. Celebrate, O Judah, your feasts, and pay your vows, for Belial will no more pass through you; he has wholly perished. For a little while I shall put off the LXX translators, because among them the very sections are also confused by the variety of their translation. And when I have briefly set out the history, I shall temper their edition with my own words. It is written in the book of Chronicles that while Sennacherib was besieging them, they could not keep the Passover in the first month; but when his army had been slain by the angel, and his flight and death had been announced, they celebrated the day of the Passover in the second month with the greatest festivity. […]

If ever there has been a most grievous persecution, such as under Valerian and Decius and Maximian, and the vengeance of the Lord has appeared upon his adversaries, let us say to the Church: LXX: Celebrate, O Judah, your feasts, pay your vows, for they will never again add to pass through into oldness; it is fulfilled, it is consummated; he has gone up breathing into your face, rescuing you from tribulation. I have said once already that according to the variety of the translation the sections themselves are also divided differently, and that the sense of the Hebrew translation cannot agree with the sections. […]

Moreover we should strive that this warning of the prophetic exhortation may not be uttered against us to no purpose: "Celebrate, O Judah, thy festivals, and pay thy vows." For if the occurrence of festival days does not interfere with the continuity of our abstinence, we shall continually enjoy spiritual festivals and so, when we cease from servile work, "there shall be month after month and Sabbath after Sabbath."
1:15.s: The First Conference of Abbot Theonas, Chapter 23

1:15.t: This is Nahum the eighth in order who was also privileged to prophesy concerning the resurrection of the Lord Christ, and he says: Feast, O Judah, keep thy feasts, perform thy vows, for they shall add to pass through thee no more. It has been consummated, it has been taken away. He went up breathing upon thy face, delivering thee from affliction.

2:1.t: He imparted the fellowship of this Holy Spirit to the apostles, for it is written, "When he had said that, he breathed upon them, and said to them, 'Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you shall retain, they are retained.' " This was the second breathing (the first had been impaired by willful sins)2 to fulfill the Scripture: "One who has been delivered from affliction has come up panting into your presence." He has been delivered from Hades. For it was after his resurrection, according to the gospel, that he breathed on them. He gives the grace at this time, and he will lavish it more abundantly. He says to them, "I am ready to give it to you even now, but the vessel cannot yet hold it. […]

LXX: Watch the way, hold the loin, be strengthened in strength exceedingly, for the Lord has turned away the insolence of Jacob, as the insolence of Israel, because those who shake out have shaken them out, and have demolished their branches. Three things are commanded to Judah. First, that he watch the way and look carefully at the road by which he is to walk, according to what is written in Jeremiah: Stand in the ways, and ask for the eternal paths, and see which is the good way, and walk in it, so that when we have stood in many ways, we may come to that way which says: I am the way. […]

He has come up who will scatter before your face, keeping the siege; watch the way, strengthen the loins, make your power very strong, for as the Lord has repaid the pride of Jacob, so the pride of Israel, because the ravagers have scattered them and have corrupted their branches. I am compelled by necessity to steer the course of my discourse between history and allegory, as between rocks and crags with shipwreck threatening, and to take care that it does not suddenly strike. For indeed, according to the fables of the poets: Scylla holds the right side, implacable Charybdis the left; if we flee the rocks, we run into the deep; if we avoid the twisting whirlpools, we are carried onto the rocks. […]

It is finished, it is taken away; he has come up breathing into your face, delivering from affliction. As it was already fixed, and in every way and altogether about to happen that Nineveh must be destroyed, he says that it is finished, indicating by this its coming to an end, as it were. And indeed also that it is taken away, that is, that it has been cut off completely and utterly destroyed. And very well indeed he says "he has come up" concerning Cyrus, signifying something emphatic, I think, such as the prophet Jeremiah also said about him, foretelling what would happen in due time to Nineveh: "A lion has come up from his den, a destroyer of nations has set out, and has gone forth from his place, to make your land a desolation, and your cities shall be laid waste, so that none […]

2:2.t: And lest perhaps you lose confidence, a reason is given you for hoping: The Lord, he says, has turned away the insolence of Jacob, as the insolence of Israel; which is ambiguous: for either the Lord has turned away the insolence of Jacob himself, with which he did injury to others, or he has turned away the insolence which Jacob endured from others. But it seems better to me that the insolence which Jacob used to do to others has been turned away by the Lord. For it is not of such great virtue to endure an injury done by others as it is of the Lord's grace to be calm, gentle and tranquil, unable to do injury. […]

Watch the road, brace your loins, be exceedingly courageous in your strength, because the Lord has turned away the insolence of Jacob, as the insolence of Israel. To those about to go very soon into Judea, and intending to go home, he necessarily adds that it is needful for the future both to watch the road and brace their loins, that is to be ready and prepared for the toils of the journey, and to be courageous against all hesitation, and to be seen to love being superior to long distances, using invincible eagerness for this. A sign of readiness is to have one's loins, as it were, well-ordered and girded. And indeed our Lord Jesus Christ says to the holy apostles, or rather to all who believe in him, "Let your loins be girded." […]

2:3.t: The shield of his mighty men is fiery, the men of the army are in scarlet; fiery are the reins of the chariot in the day of his preparation, and the charioteers have been lulled to sleep. They have been thrown into confusion on the roads; the four-horse chariots have been dashed together in the streets. Their appearance is like torches, like lightnings running to and fro. He will remember his mighty men; they will fall on their roads; swiftly they will go up to her walls, and a shelter will be prepared. The gates of the rivers have been opened, and the temple has been torn down to the ground, and the soldier has been led away captive, and her handmaids were driven along, moaning like doves, murmuring in their hearts. […]

Now let us come to the Seventy translators. Those who shake out, who shook out Jacob and Israel and scattered their shoots, also broke the arms which they had been accustomed to have while they were insolent, and with which they had oppressed all the weak; and they did not do this only, but they also destroyed in fire the mighty men who were mocking. Consider whether you can call the mighty men mocking in fire the opposing powers, which serve the fiery darts of the devil, which, mighty and once mocking Jacob and Israel in fire, had chariots and horses, by which they were borne, urged on, into war in the day of their preparation. […]

2:4.t: And returning again to the order of the description, he says: So great is the multitude of those coming that the column on the march is mingled together and cannot be told apart. The four-horse chariots themselves too, while they cannot find a way, are dashed against one another in the streets because of the multitude. The appearance of the Babylonians is like torches, like lightnings running to and fro, so that they terrify their adversaries by the sight before they lay them low with the sword.

2:5.t: Then Asshur will remember his mighty men and will look for those who fell on the roads, and he will swiftly go up the walls of Nineveh, and because of the very long siege he will prepare shelters to ward off the heat.

And when the devil and all his nobles have understood this, they will remember the consummation which had long ago been foretold, and they will flee in the days. For they will by no means move about in the nights, but as the day grows bright the darkness will be put to flight, and they will grow weak on the way, not making progress nor fulfilling their endeavors, and they will hasten to the walls. For so great a terror of the coming Lord will seize them, and so feeble will they be for resisting, that they will flee to the bounds of the world, by which the world is shut in and encircled as by walls, and they will prepare themselves to resist. […]

2:6.t: But is this the only place we read of "substance"? Has it not also been said in another passage: "The gates of the cities are broken down, the mountains are fallen, and his substance is revealed"? What, does the word mean something created here also? Some, I know, are accustomed to say that the substance is substance in money. Then, if you give this meaning to the word, the mountains fell in order that someone's possessions of money might be seen. But let us remember what mountains fell, those, namely, of which it has been said, "If you shall have faith as a grain of mustard seed you shall say to this mountain, 'Be removed, and be cast into the sea!' " By mountains, then, are meant high things that exalt themselves.

But what does it profit to build a house unless the Lord has built it? What does it help to shut the gates which the Lord unbars? The gates of Nineveh have been opened, which had a multitude of citizens like rivers, and the temple, that is, her kingdom, has been destroyed, and the soldier has been led away captive, that is, all have been led into Babylon. But by the handmaids of Nineveh understand, by a metaphor, the lesser cities and villages and forts. Or certainly the captive women will be driven along before the faces of the victors; and so great will be the terror that their grief will not even break out into sobbing and wailing, but they will moan silently within themselves and with a dark murmur swallow their tears, after the manner of cooing doves. […]

But while they are thinking this, all the things which had been held and possessed by them will be brought out into the open, and the gates which they had shut will be opened, and their kingdoms will fall, and the substance, that is, the riches, will be uncovered. But the substance of the world itself and all her handmaids, after they have subjected themselves to Christ and have begun to serve him, will be led glad and rejoicing, and believing from the inmost heart of confession, so that they are compared to the cleanness of doves, they will murmur or speak in their hearts. And then will be fulfilled what is said in the sixty-seventh (68th) psalm of the victory of the Savior: Ascending on high, he led captivity captive.

2:8.t: But since we have once said that Nineveh is the beautiful one, that is, the world, let us see what the pool of the world is. Scripture does not say that the waters of Nineveh are like the waters of the sea, nor like the waters of rivers, nor like the waters of springs, nor like the waters of wells, but like the waters of a pool, so that, just as in Jeremiah the people is rebuked which forsook the fountain of living water and dug for itself broken cisterns that cannot hold water, so in Nineveh too all those waters are such as have fallen from heaven and, leaving their ancient height, have slipped down to the depths. […]

And Nineveh: like a pool of waters are her waters, but they have fled. Stand, stand, and there is none who turns back; plunder the silver, plunder the gold, and there is no end of riches from all the desirable vessels. LXX: And Nineveh: like a pool of waters are her waters, and they, fleeing, did not stand, and there was none who looked back; they were plundering the silver, they were plundering the gold, and there was no end of her adornment; she has been weighed down above all the vessels of her concupiscence. […]

2:9.t: And as for what is said: They were plundering the silver, they were plundering the gold, and there was no end of her adornment: she has been weighed down above all the vessels of her concupiscence, it is said of the waters of Nineveh, and of those fleeing who had fled and did not stand, nor was there one who looked back; and who, not content only to have fled and not to have looked back, were plundering the silver besides, whatever eloquence was seen in the world; they were plundering the gold, whatever was splendid in the way of maxims in the learning of the age, in order to adorn Nineveh, in order to compose their dogmas with every flower of thoughts and words. Because of this Nineveh has been weighed down above all the vessels of her concupiscence; […]

2:10.t: She has been scattered and torn and rent apart, and the heart is melting, and there is a loosening of the knees and a failing in all the kidneys, and the faces of all are like the blackness of a pot. LXX: A shaking out, a shaking out again, and a boiling up, and a breaking of heart and a loosening of knees, and pains upon every loin, and the faces too of all like the scorching of a pot. Under the metaphor of a captive woman, Nineveh is described as scattered, torn, rent: her heart melting, her knees loosened, and her kidneys broken, and the faces of all her inhabitants, through terror of the enemy and the greatness of their fear, appear scorched like pots, wasted, and disfigured with pallor. […]

2:11.t: But since according to ἀναγωγὴν (anagogy), both in Jonah and in this prophet, we have interpreted Nineveh as this world, and according to John: The whole world is set in the evil one, when the world, the dwelling of beasts and the place in which lions used to pasture, has passed away, then in wonder and exultation we shall say: Where is the dwelling of the lions and the pasture of the lions' whelps, to which the lion went, the devil, of whom Peter also speaks: Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour, and the lion's whelp, the antichrist, and all perverse teachings, the contrary word? You have heard, says John, that antichrist is coming; but now there are many antichrists; for there are as many antichrists as there are false dogmas. […]

Where is the dwelling of the lions, and the pasture of the lions' whelps, to which the lion went, that the lion's whelp might enter there, and there is none to frighten them? The lion took enough for his whelps, and killed for his lionesses; and he filled his caves with prey, and his den with plunder. For caves and lionesses the Seventy translated nests and whelps; in the rest the sense is the same. But this is still said of Nineveh: that it was the dwelling of kings and the court of nobles, to which the lion went, the Babylonian king, that is, Nebuchadnezzar, and the lion's whelp, that is, his under-kings as well, and there was none to resist them. The lion took enough for his whelps, and killed for his lionesses. […]

2:12.t: This lion, before he was killed by Christ, took very many as prey for his whelps, and killed for his young lions, his attendants, that is, the demons. Look at the conventicles of the heretics, and you will not have to seek the many taken by the lion. Consider the dead who have left life behind, and you will not call their churches the sheepfold of the shepherd, but the caves of the lion, which he has filled with corpses and the blood of the dead. You have made, says David, darkness, and it became night; in it all the beasts of the forest will pass through. The lions' whelps, to snatch and to seek their food from God. […]

2:13.t: Behold, I am against you, says the Lord of hosts, and I will burn your chariots even to smoke; and the sword will devour your whelps, and I will cut off your prey from the earth, and the voice of your messengers will be heard no more. LXX: Behold, I am against you, says the Lord Almighty, and I will burn your multitude in smoke, and the sword will devour your lions, and I will take away your prey from the earth, and your works will be heard no more. O Nineveh, all that has been said you will suffer, and I am its author. I the Lord will burn your chariots even to smoke and consumption, and I will cause all your nobles and under-kings to be devoured by the sword. No longer will you lay waste lands, nor exact tributes, nor will your emissaries be heard throughout the provinces; […]

3:1.t: Let us mourn with Nahum, and say with him, "Woe to him that buildeth his house on high." Or rather let us mourn for them as Christ mourned for those of old. "Woe to you that are rich, for ye have received your consolation." Let us, I beseech you, not cease thus lamenting, and if it be not unseemly, let us even beat our breasts for the carelessness of our brethren. Let us not weep for him who is already dead, but let us weep for the rapacious man, the grasping, the covetous, the insatiable. Why should we mourn for the dead, in whose case it is impossible henceforth to effect anything? Let us mourn for these who are capable even of change.

Woe, city of bloods, all full of the laceration of falsehood; plunder will not depart from you. The voice of the whip, and the voice of the onrush of the wheel, and of the snorting horse, and of the seething chariot, and of the horseman going up, and of the flashing sword, of the gleaming spear, and of the multitude slain and of heavy ruin; and there is no end of corpses, and they will fall upon their own bodies. Because of the multitude of the fornications of the harlot, beautiful and pleasing and having sorceries, who sold nations in her fornications, and families in her sorceries. LXX: O city of bloods, all lying, full of iniquity, the hunt will not be handled; […]

These things have been said of Nineveh in the simple sense. But if, on account of the name of beauty, we have reasonably understood Nineveh as the world, rightly the world, which is set in evil, is called a city of bloods, because of the multitude of archers and of those who kill men with their tongues as with swords. Hence, consequently, it is also all lying, which refers to the perversity of the teachings, since the word of God has nowhere in it to lay its head, while perverse dogmas possess everything. There is none who understands or seeks God; all have turned aside, together they have become useless; there is none who does good, there is not even one. […]

Woe to the bloody city, all full of lies and injustice. He has called it a city of blood; for those who had reigned in Nineveh were most ready for murder and exceedingly bloodthirsty; and those in it were otherwise warlike, and always eager to make their attacks untamable against whomever they might go. And he says "full of lies," because it was also full of idols, in which falsehood is especially not unproven. For they are falsely named, and the handmade gods steal the glory of divinity, "Silver and gold, according to what is written, the works of men's hands." And the wise Jeremiah somewhere also called it a land of graven images. […]

3:2.t: But the voice of whips too is heard in the world, since many are the tribulations of the just, and those who are scourged by them cry out and testify with a tearful voice to the greatness of their pain: when one is seized by a demon, another by anger, which is like madness, another by lust, hatred, envy, pride, the whip of the Assyrian king sounds in them. And in the ills of the body too we understand the whip of the devil, of which it is said to the just man: And the whip will not come near your tent; if ever we see this man rotted with jaundice and outliving his own corpse, another with water under the skin swimming in a swollen body, and, as the limbs grow, the form of the former man shrinking, as we lately saw in the Hydra; […]

The voice of the whip of an empire ever cruel and raging, and the voice of the onrush of the wheel. Let us take voice for sound; the seething wheel, a running about in different directions, and of the snorting horse and of the seething chariot: in all of them voice is understood. So beautiful, according to the Hebrew, and so like a painting is the description of an army preparing itself for battle, that every word of mine would be poorer. For what he says, And of heavy ruin, and there is no end of corpses, let us understand of the adversaries who were slain by them. And they will fall upon their own bodies: either they will fall from their own multitude, while they are crowded together by one another, or they will fall upon the corpses of the slain; […]

Because emptying they have emptied them out and their branches. They destroyed the weapons of their power from among men, mighty men mocking in fire. The reins of their chariots on the day of his preparation, and the horsemen shall be thrown into confusion in the ways, and the chariots shall be thrown into confusion and shall clash together in the broad ways; their appearance is like torches of fire and like lightnings running to and fro. As the God who knows all things sounded in the holy prophets the things that would be at various times, they necessarily announced them according to what seemed good to him. And many times they occurred even in the very visions of things. Therefore they were astonished, and seeing them all but fulfilled, they made their pronouncements about them; […]
3:2.s: Commentary on the Twelve Minor Prophets

3:3.t: And the voice of the horseman going up also resounds in her, who, prepared for war by a certain art and by wheeling, advances not without danger to the one fighting against him. This horseman has the sword of speech, sharpened on the whetstone of dialectic and smoothed with the oil of the rhetorical art; he has gleaming arms, as Satan transforms himself into an angel of light, arms which are contrary to the apostolic armor. Nor is it any wonder if there is a multitude of the wounded in Nineveh, since there is a multitude of arrows. And just as the four with which we fight and are protected are the shields of the virtues, prudence, justice, temperance, fortitude, so on the contrary there are four vices, folly, iniquity, luxury, fear, by which we are struck by the enemy. […]

3:4.t: Because of the multitude, he says, of the fornications of the harlot, since she fornicated with many nations, and worshiped the idols of the whole world which she had subjected to herself. Beautiful and pleasing, and having sorceries: it means magicians; who sold nations in her fornications, and families in her sorceries, that is, she who had power over all the nations.

In this place the LXX translators, although we have put, according to the Hebrew, Because of the multitude of the fornications of the harlot, wanted, as it were, another beginning, so as to say: For the multitude of fornication, and, the sentence being finished there, then to begin: A harlot beautiful and pleasing, leader of sorceries. For leader of sorceries Aquila and Symmachus translated, having sorceries. Nor will anyone wonder that Nineveh is now the most pleasing of harlots, who has seen so great a multitude of men fornicating with her, and almost all being drawn to love of her by her sorceries and by certain incantations. She sold nations in her fornications, nations which take the members of Christ and make them the members of a harlot, and tribes in her sorceries. […]

3:5.t: Behold, I am against you, says the Lord Almighty; because I am almighty, I can heal all diseases, and what is impossible for others is possible for me. I will lay bare your hinder parts in your face, that is, my virtues, precepts and words, which you have cast behind your back: though you do not deserve it, I will make you see them. For I had commanded you concerning my words, that they should always move before your eyes, be bound on and hang there. But you, scorning the command of him who gave it, left them behind your footsteps, so that you not only did not do what I had commanded, but did not even deign to look at it. Or certainly I will make you see and understand your errors, which before, when you were borne along blind and headlong, you thought to be virtues. […]

Behold, I am against you, says the Lord of hosts, and I will lay bare your shameful parts before your face, and I will show the nations your nakedness, and the kingdoms your disgrace; and I will cast abominations upon you, and I will heap insults upon you, and I will make you an example. LXX: Behold, I am against you, says the Lord Almighty, and I will uncover your hinder parts over your face, and I will show the nations your shame, and the kingdoms your disgrace; and I will cast abomination upon you according to your uncleannesses, and I will make you an example. Because you have sold nations, O Nineveh, in your fornications, and families in your sorceries, and like a public brothel have spread your feet for all, therefore I myself will come to you to overthrow you; […]

3:6.t: And I will cast abomination upon you according to your uncleannesses, so that, as you are unclean, so you may be seen to be unclean, and may not deceive very many who, cleaving to you before, were made one body with you. And I will make you an example, so that the dreaded likeness of the punishment may forbid the likeness of the sinning.

3:7.t: And it shall be: everyone who sees you will spring back from you and will say: Nineveh is laid waste. Who will shake the head over you? Whence shall I seek a consoler for you? In the Hebrew the word head is not found, but we added it, so that the sense might become clearer. Indeed, Symmachus translated it thus: And everyone who sees you will withdraw from you and will say. Nineveh is torn apart, who will mourn with her? The Seventy, moreover: And it shall be, everyone who sees you will go down from you and will say: Wretched Nineveh, who will groan for her? Whence shall I seek consolation for her, tuning the string. […]

3:8.t: For what is read in the Seventy, Tune, or set in order, the string, is still said to Nineveh. And the sense is: What is disordered and out of tune in you, and jarring in different directions, tune like strings, Nineveh, for your beauty and your greatness, which you believe you possess in a pre-eminent degree, will profit you nothing unless you tune yourself for singing. For consider the whole part of the lot of the sons of Ammon, and how whatever goods they are reckoned to possess did not defend them from going into captivity and from their little ones being dashed in the ways. What did the rivers profit her, beside which the city of Ammon is set? […]

Are you better than Amon, which dwells among the rivers? Water is round about her, whose riches are the sea, waters are her walls; Ethiopia is her strength, and Egypt, and there is no end; Africa and the Libyans were your help. Yet she too is led away into exile, into captivity; her little ones will be dashed at the head of all the ways, and over her renowned ones they will cast lots; and all her nobles will be fastened in fetters. And you therefore will be drunk and will be despised; and you will seek your help from the enemy; all your fortresses, like fig trees with their early figs, if they are shaken, will fall into the mouth of the eater. […]

Let these things be said παραφραστικῶς (by way of paraphrase) according to the Seventy translators: for we have once for all resolved to follow the common edition too, lest we seem to have given the Hydra and Sardanapalus any occasion for censure. However, the example of the overthrow of Nineveh does not seem to me to fit well enough with the sons of Lot, who are called Amman. For first, it is called Ammon and not Amman; then Ammana, which is now called Philadelphia, is not set upon rivers, nor is its wealth gathered from the sea, since it is inland; nor are waters its walls, nor does it have Ethiopia and Egypt and Africa and the Libyans as allies; […]

But since we have interpreted Nineveh also as this world, she is commanded to tune and set in order her strings and to prepare herself for a mournful song; for the part of the sons of Ammon, which had been much better than Nineveh and had dwelt upon rivers, because it was caught in error, has paid the penalty of its crime. And first, as must be said according to the history of Alexandria, Ammon means peoples, and the sense according to the laws of allegory is this: Consider the peoples of the Church, which dwells upon the streams of the prophets, and has teachers round about her, out of whose belly rivers flow, and whose beginning is the sea. […]

But if we wish to interpret Ammon of the sons of Lot, let us say that Lot had two sons by his two daughters, Moab and Ammon, of whom the elder, Moab, means 'from the father' or 'paternal water', and the younger, Ammon, either 'son of my race' or 'our people'. And I think that, just as to one who had been born of Judah it is said because of his sin: Seed of Canaan, and not of Judah, and in Ezekiel to sinful Jerusalem: Your root and your generation are from the land of Canaan, your father an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite, so whoever were of the former people, that is, of the Jews, and of the younger, that is, of ours, are figuratively called Moabites and Ammonites. […]

3:9.t: What protection did Ethiopia and Egypt, once her allies, afford her? As, then, the help of her allies did not aid her, so neither will there be an end of your fleeing, O Nineveh, but you will be laid waste hither and thither. Why should I speak of the Ethiopians and the Egyptians, who were the protectors of the sons of Ammon, when even the Libyans were her allies?

Moreover, what we passed over, And there is no end of your flight, since it is said to Nineveh and is set among the things written about Ammon, and seems to be inserted irregularly in a place not its own, let us refer to Nineveh as if by ὑπέρβατον (hyperbaton), so that the order is: And you will be drunk, and there is no end of your flight, and you will be despised, and the rest that is said to Nineveh. And we will interpret it to mean that there is no end of Nineveh's flight from God, because she always makes progress in fleeing and never wishes to stand still, according to what we said above: And they, fleeing, did not stand, and there was none to look back. […]

3:10.t: She too, therefore, whom my discourse, says the prophet, describes, will be taken by the Babylonian king, and the same man will be the devastator both of you and of her. These things Josephus too, the writer of the Jewish history, relates in his books: Her little ones will be dashed at the crossroads; her nobles will be divided by the lot of the victors, and princes once most powerful will be led captive in chains.

She too, therefore, will be led into captivity; her little ones, because they will not be able to walk, will be slain in the ways, struck down before the faces of their parents, and all her wealth will perhaps be divided by the victors. Nor will any of her princes escape, for they will be bound with iron and fetters.

She too, therefore, if she does not take heed to herself and keep her heart with all diligence, will be led captive and will mourn her sons. Her little ones too, who are still at the beginnings of the ways and have not reached the middle of the journey, will be dashed at their very beginnings, and the most savage enemies will hasten to divide among themselves by lot all her splendid things, and they will drag into captivity her nobles, whom we can understand as princes and overseers, bound with chains and hampered by the heaviest weight of fetters.

3:11.t: Since, then, Alexandria is to suffer these things, you too, O Nineveh, will drink from the same cup, and will be drunk, and lying stupefied you will be despised, and you will come into such need that you will ask help from the Babylonians, or against the Babylonians, from your enemies.

And you therefore, O Nineveh, will be drunk, and you who were once rich and beautiful, who had so many lovers, will be despised by all, and with your enemies pursuing you will seek rest and will not find it.

And you therefore, Nineveh, that is, unbelieving men, men clinging wholly to the world, will feel punishments and will be stupefied by my cup, since those too have drunk who had been of my portion and fell by their own fault. And you will be despised by me; you will seek an end amid the vices and passions that will press upon you, and nonetheless you will not be able to find a resting place and an end of evils; but all your desires and delights, and the powers of the age, and the dogmas you seemed to yourself to hold most firmly, will be devoured by the eater, of whom Samson speaks in a parable: Out of the eater came forth food, and out of the strong came forth sweetness. […]

3:12.t: All your strongholds, and your walls stretched up on high, and the heights of your towers, which you now think impregnable, and your brave men and warriors, will be compared to first-ripe figs, which, if they are shaken with a light touch, will fall into the mouth of the devourer.

All your warriors and all your auxiliaries will be a prey to the enemies, and will be taken without any labor, like the early figs of a fig tree, which, when shaken, fall not to the ground, so that there may not be even the small labor of gathering them, but straightway into the mouth of the devourer.

3:13.t: These things, as I said, have been said by us briefly so that the sense may be grasped; now, returning to the beginning of the section, let us unfold each point as we can. Who would not say that beautiful Nineveh, a soul beautiful by nature, beguiled by the luxury and pleasures of this age, has come to womanish delights, and, her manliness lost, has languished into a woman? For if the soul of the righteous man, coming to the perfect man and keeping the firmness of its creation, and cleaving to God, is made one spirit with him, why should not, on the contrary, the soul that loves the world become one with the world, and, reduced to womanly softness, lose its manly firmness? […]

These things I have explained more plainly according to the Hebrew, treading in the very footsteps of Scripture, for the reader's easier understanding. But I will speak also according to the LXX, following the τροπολογίαν (tropology) I have begun, first briefly, that is, as in an epitome, and afterwards discussing each point more broadly: Your people, O Nineveh, that is, the men of this age, who are properly called the people of the Assyrian city, are so unnerved by passions and have so languished in vices that they are compared to the weakness of women; for they possess nothing strong in their souls, nothing robust and manly. Hence the enemies, prevailing against them, have opened all their senses and have entered through the bodily doors. […]

Behold, your people are women in the midst of you; to your enemies the gates of your land will be thrown wide open; fire will devour your bars. Draw yourself water because of the siege, build up your fortifications; go into the clay, and tread it, and working it hold the brick. There fire will devour you; you will perish by the sword; it will devour you like the cankerworm; gather yourself like the cankerworm, multiply like the locust. You have made your tradings more than the stars of heaven are. The cankerworm spread out, and flew away. Your guards are like the locust, and your little ones like the locusts of locusts, which settle in the hedges on the day of cold. The sun has risen, and they have flown away, and their place where they were is not known. […]

3:14.t: Also, Draw to yourself water of the fortification, is said of the word of God, so that the soul may surround herself with the teaching and reason of the Scriptures as with a most firm wall, lest the enemy be able to break into her inner parts. Hold, he says, your fortifications. Whatever good you have in you by nature, which preserves in you the beginning given by the best Creator, this, unhappy soul, Nineveh, hold for your defense, and do not let it flow out of the ruling part of the heart. As for what is added after this, Walk into the clay, and be trodden in the straw, another perhaps may think it is said of the soul which, fixed in the clay of the body and the straw of this world, empty, that is, and perishable, turning itself about wholly, is trodden down by demons. […]

3:15.t: Then follows: There fire will eat you. If you are not over the brick and do not have dominion over the flesh, but remain in the brick, and love the straw, and live in the flesh according to the flesh, not only will the burning darts of the enemy devour you, but his sword too will kill you, and like locusts it will consume with greedy tooth whatever in you seemed green and sprouting of its own accord from the good of nature, and as the cankerworm, its flight lost and weighed down by its own weight, so you too, weighed down by the burden of sins, will be dragged down to the earth. Therefore, lest you suffer such and so great things, multiply like the cankerworm, and as great as its number is, so many virtues must you have. […]

3:16.t: However, you will not be able to hesitate to call cankerworm the multitude of men which, going along the broad way, busies itself in the world, when you see them wholly given to the earth, running about hither and thither with fickleness of opinion, and unable to fly to higher things. Look at Rome, and at Constantinople exchanging its former poverty together with its earlier name. See Alexandria, the head of Egypt, and when a riot has been stirred up, either for scarcity of the grain supply or, what is matter for shame and blushing, on account of charioteers and mimes and actors, see the people rush like the cankerworm and, clinging wholly to vices, flit hither and thither through its fickleness and its change of opinion from moment to moment; […]

Above, according to the Hebrew, I had come as far as the place where it says: The sun has risen, and they have flown away, and their place where they were is not known. And I said what seemed to me in the context of the discourse itself. Now, because the LXX seem to have the beginning of a sense of their own, I will set down their testimony and follow the order of the explanation I have begun.

LXX: The cankerworm rushed in and flew out; your commingled one leapt out like the attelabus, like the locust that goes up upon the hedge on the day of frost; the sun rose, and it leapt out, and did not know its place. It seems to me that the multitude of Nineveh, without a ruler, mingled together from here and there without order, and rushing wherever impulse carries it, is compared to the cankerworm, a small and innumerable creature, which seems to raise itself only a little from the ground. And the attelabus too, which in Greek is called συμμικτὸς and in Latin has been translated as 'commingled one', we can understand as the ignoble rabble and a people gathered from here and there out of diverse nations, that is, not citizens but foreigners. […]

3:17.t: Moreover, as to what follows, The attelabus leapt out, and your mixed one like the locust, I think the mixed one differs from the cankerworm in this, that the cankerworm is compared to the unskilled and innumerable multitude, but the mixed one is gathered from here and there out of all nations. And just as in cities some are citizens and others foreigners, who are pleased to live in a city not their own, so I think that the mixed one who dwells in Nineveh are those who seem to themselves, in their own opinion, to follow some dogmas of truth, and to be better than the cankerworm in this, that the cankerworm does nothing else but stay always on the ground and, without wings, serve its food and its belly; […]

3:18.t: Your shepherds have slumbered, king of Asshur; your princes will be buried, your people is scattered upon the mountains, and there is none to gather them. Your crushing is not obscure, most grievous is your stroke. All who have heard the report of you have clenched the hand over you, for upon whom has your malice not passed continually? LXX: Woe to them. Your shepherds have slumbered, the king of Asshur has lulled your mighty ones to sleep, your people has gone away upon the mountains, and there was none to receive them, and there is no healing for your crushing; your stroke swells. All who have heard the news of you will clap their hands over you, for upon whom has your malice not rushed continually? […]

Woe, therefore, to those who are masters of perverse doctrines in Nineveh. And fittingly it is said to them: Your shepherds have slumbered; for they have given sleep to their eyes, and slumber to their eyelids. And therefore they did not find a place for the Lord, nor a tabernacle for the God of Jacob. Nor did they hear of Ephrathah, that is, the fruitful Church, nor did they find it in the thickets of the woods. But not only have the shepherds of this mixed one, and of the locust, which, when frost threatens, sits in the hedges, slumbered, but they have also been lulled to sleep by the king of the Assyrians. For the Assyrian king knows that he cannot deceive the sheep unless he has first lulled the shepherds to sleep. It is ever the devil's endeavor to lull wakeful souls to sleep. […]

But according to the Hebrew as well, before we discuss the edition of the Seventy — for in them the sense is far other and different —, we ought to climb a little from the history to the heights, and to teach that in the last prophecy of Nahum an ἀποστροφὴ (apostrophe) is made to the devil, the great sense, the prince of the Assyrians, who once said boastfully: By strength I will do it, and by the wisdom of understanding I will take away the bounds of the nations, and I will feed upon their strength, and I will shake the cities that are inhabited, and that it is said to him: O Lucifer, who rose in the morning, who sent your sparks to all the nations, how have you fallen to the earth and been crushed? […]

3:19.t: Your wound is not obscure, nor is it such a stroke as could be cured by a physician's hand. All who hear that Nineveh has been overthrown and the Assyrian king overcome, and that the most mighty city, and the king once lord of the city, has been wounded, and lies half-dead, and wallows in his own blood, will either be stunned at the greatness of the event and the unhoped-for news, and will clench their hands, or surely, for the greatness of their joy, insulting you, they will clap their hands and resound with a kind of clamor of joy. For there is no one who can grieve over you and grant tears to your overthrow and your wound, since there is no one over whom your malice has not continually passed. […]

There follows: There is no healing for your crushing; your stroke swells. Therefore the mixed one of Nineveh cannot be healed, because he does not lay aside his pride, and the wound is always fresh, and he is struck every day as the devil smites him. And after all these things there is no healing for his crushing; for although he seems to himself to be sound, yet his soul is broken and crushed, as the hammer of the whole earth strikes from above, and it is not healed, because it is always lifted up. But if he is humbled and submits himself to Christ: A crushed and humbled heart God does not despise, and: A sacrifice to God is an afflicted spirit. At the end is placed: All who have heard the news of you will clap their hands over you. […]
